source.title: VSA: Faster Video Diffusion with Trainable Sparse Attention
source.authors: Pei-Yuan Zhang; Yongqi Chen; Hao-Feng Huang; Will Lin; Zhengzhong Liu; Ion Stoica; E. Xing; Hao Zhang

record.tranche_reason: The study reports a scaling sweep of video diffusion transformers, extending scaling-loss measurements to a different modality and training regime than language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The paper cites established scaling laws when choosing an ablation compute budget, but does not test held-out language-model cross-entropy, small-run extrapolation, or parameter/token allocation. Its own video-DiT scaling sweep is relevant to V5. Other reported ablations and generation-quality results do not test whether loss follows a power law.
record.test_reason: The study builds a sparse-attention method (VSA) for video DiTs. Its scaling sweep (60M–1.4B parameters, up to 4×10^21 FLOPS) serves to compare VSA's Pareto frontier with full attention's. The text never states the fitted functional form, exponents or goodness of fit, and never argues that video-DiT loss follows a power law. The scaling results rest on the established laws as an evaluation tool and report the authors' own method's advantage, so they do not test V5 or any other version. Established laws are also used only to pick the ablation compute budget.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors conclude that VSA matches full-attention diffusion loss at 2.53× lower training FLOPS across 60M–1.4B models and budgets up to 4e21 FLOPS, retains generation quality when retrofitted into Wan2.1 with a 1.7× end-to-end speedup, and is a practical, scalable alternative to full attention.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures video-diffusion training loss and scaling, rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy and the original studies' parameter/token/compute scaling setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that the optimal sparse-attention Top-K depends on sequence length and training compute; this is sparsity sensitivity, not a test of fitted loss exponents or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.

fits_no_version.finding: Fitted loss-vs-compute curves for VSA and full-attention video DiTs (60M–1.4B) are parallel, implying a constant 2.53× training-FLOPS saving across scales.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Attention sparsity shifts the video-DiT compute scaling curve by a constant factor without changing its slope.

fits_no_version.finding: The optimal Top-K sparsity depends on sequence length and training compute; K=32 overtakes K=16 at 61440 length once compute reaches 1e21 FLOPS.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal attention sparsity is an additional axis of compute-optimal scaling and decreases (denser attention) as compute grows.

record.problems: The scaling-curve values and fitted exponents are not stated in the text; Figure 2(b) is supplied only as a figure reference here. No uncertainty estimates for the scaling results are stated.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported result directly tests a claim version. The 410M VSA-versus-full-attention loss comparison and generation-quality evaluations do not establish a scaling form. The reported dependence of optimal attention Top-K on sequence length and compute concerns sparsity allocation, not the parameter/token allocation in V3.

untested.parts: Whether video-diffusion loss follows a power law in parameters or compute: curves are 'fitted', but the form, exponents and fit quality are unstated. Image models, repeated data, and fine-tuning/transfer regimes are not studied.
Only an informal observation used to set the ablation budget: at 4.5e20 FLOPS, a 120M model beats a 60M model. No allocation trend is fitted.
Shape is not varied at fixed parameter count.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'supports' label for V5 is removed. The paper never establishes a power-law form: the fitted curves have no stated functional form or exponents, and the scaling sweep evaluates the authors' own method against a baseline. The Top-K/compute finding could be added as a row if sparsity-scaling claims are tracked.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute is not tested.
No power law fitted on small runs is used to predict and evaluate much larger runs.
The study does not test a stable compute-optimal allocation trend for parameter count and token count.
Depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count are not varied to test their effect on loss.

Video diffusion scaling is tested, but image models and power-law scaling in repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer regimes are not tested. The paper does not state fitted exponents for the video-DiT curves.
No downstream-task performance scaling or prediction from pretraining loss is tested.
The study does not test dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation on fitting choices, nor whether curves bend away from a power law.

rows.subject: Video DiTs trained with VSA (scaling sweep; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared diffusion-loss scaling across model sizes and training-compute budgets; the text describes fitted curves and a Pareto frontier.
rows.measure: Diffusion loss across model sizes and compute budgets; fitted scaling curves/Pareto frontier
rows.note: Aggregate sweep across the stated model-size range. The text says VSA has a better Pareto frontier than full attention and that the fitted curves are parallel, but does not specify the fitted functional form or exponents; therefore the specific power-law form is not established in the supplied text.
rows.check: The row compares the study's own method (VSA) with full attention via Pareto frontiers; the stated result is 'parallel fitted curves', meaning a constant 2.53× FLOPS saving. The fitted form and exponents are never given and the figure values are unreadable in the text, so the row cannot show whether loss follows a power law. It is a method-vs-baseline comparison, not a test of V5.

relation.reason: §3.1 explicitly uses established scaling laws; §3.2 reports VSA's comparative loss and compute savings without specifying the fitted functional form or exponents.

tranche.reason: Uses established scaling laws to guide compute allocation and compares its sparse-attention method with full attention; does not establish a power-law form or test another claim version.

source_check.notes: The text states a 2.53× training-FLOPS reduction across the scaling sweep, but provides no numerical diffusion-loss values for Figure 2(b). Parallel fitted curves alone do not establish V5's power-law form.
